title: Passkeys: what they fix and what stays open
body_md:
## A card coded for one room

At a hotel desk the clerk codes a keycard for your room. Hold it to the door next to yours and the lock blinks red: the card works only where it was made to work. A passkey behaves the same way, with a website’s identity standing in for the room.

Technically it is a WebAuthn credential for one particular service, built on a public key and a private one. At registration the service keeps the public key. At sign-in your authenticator answers a fresh challenge from the service using the private key, which is never sent to the service. Because the credential is tied to the service’s identifier, a lookalike site cannot collect a valid response for the real one, as long as WebAuthn is implemented correctly. That protects the sign-in exchange. It does not judge anything you do after you are in.

“Passkey” does not promise a single way of storing it. Some credentials stay on a physical key or on one device; others sync through a platform or a credential manager, and then the provider decides how the synced copy is protected and recovered. Your face or fingerprint usually opens the authenticator on the device, and the site gets proof that you signed in, never an image of your face or finger. A device PIN can open it too, so a weak screen lock or a shared device counts. Some services use a passkey in place of the password, others as an extra factor. Find out which kind you are dealing with.

### Setting one up, and signing in from another device

Create a passkey only from the service’s settings, opened by you, and only on a device you control. If the service lets you name the device, do so, then test a fresh sign-in. Sometimes a phone can approve a sign-in on a computer through a QR code on the screen. That lends the computer your phone’s approval for one login; it does not copy the key onto the computer. If a passkey prompt appears when you did not ask for one, cancel it and open the service yourself. A QR code is a way into a procedure and says nothing about whether the page around it can be trusted.

### When the phone goes missing

List where each passkey lives, whether it syncs, and what happens if that device or its sync account is out of reach. Protect the sync account and the device, and keep a backup method the service supports. If a device is lost, revoke its passkey or session in the real service and follow the platform’s procedure for lost devices. Do not assume that losing one platform account loses every passkey: a separate hardware key or another synced provider may still hold one. The reverse holds too: a passkey does not necessarily retire the old password, the SMS recovery or a help-desk reset. Look at those routes as part of the upgrade.

widget_config.goal: Register and test a passkey, knowing where it is stored, what puts that device at risk and how you would recover the account.
widget_config.today_action: Pick a service that offers passkeys and open its sign-in settings yourself. Create a passkey on a personal device, test a fresh sign-in, and note the backup method and how to remove the passkey.
widget_config.scope: A general explanation of WebAuthn; the Google steps apply only to Google accounts. Storage, sync and fallback routes vary by service and provider. The cases and exercises are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: A passkey offer at the library
blocks.situation: You are signed in to a travel site on a library computer when it offers “Create a passkey.” The browser suggests saving it on this machine.
blocks.analysis: Do not register a credential on a computer you do not control. Wait for your own device, or use your own phone if the site supports approving a sign-in from it, and sign out of the library machine before you leave.

blocks.title: A QR code you asked for
blocks.situation: You opened your account from your own bookmark and started the sign-in yourself. Your laptop now shows a QR code so that the phone beside it can approve the login, and the account page is the one you expect.
blocks.analysis: This is probably the legitimate cross-device WebAuthn flow. Make sure the page that started it is the one you opened, look at the prompt on your phone, then approve there. What you are trusting is the service you opened yourself and the action you expected. The QR code proves nothing on its own.

blocks.title: Add a passkey, keep your access
blocks.setup: Four separate moments with an invented account on a learning platform. Each moment says what has already happened, so a choice in one does not leave a passkey behind for the next.

steps.prompt: Moment 1: the platform supports passkeys, and a setup QR code arrives out of the blue. Where do you start the registration?

choices.text: Open the platform yourself, sign in and go to its account security settings.
choices.consequence: The passkey is created for the service you meant.
choices.explanation: Registering something this sensitive never needs an invitation link.

choices.text: Scan the setup QR code from the unexpected message.
choices.consequence: A page you know nothing about gets to decide what happens next.
choices.explanation: A QR code does not vouch for whatever is behind it.

steps.prompt: Moment 2: you are in your own account’s settings, which you opened yourself, and the browser asks where to save the new passkey. What matters?

choices.text: Pick the shared family laptop, since it is within reach.
choices.consequence: Anyone who gets past its lock may be able to sign in as you.
choices.explanation: Register passkeys only on devices you control.

choices.text: Pick your own authenticator, and note whether it syncs or stays on the device.
choices.consequence: You know which account or device has to survive for your next sign-in.
choices.explanation: How a passkey is stored and backed up depends on the provider.

steps.prompt: Moment 3: you have created a passkey on your own device and tested it on the real platform. What is the next check?

choices.text: Look at which old passwords, MFA methods and recovery routes the service still accepts.
choices.consequence: You can see every way in that remains.
choices.explanation: Adding a passkey does not automatically close the older routes.

choices.text: Assume the platform has switched off its password and SMS recovery.
choices.consequence: A weaker route may still be open.
choices.explanation: Read the actual settings instead of assuming the move is finished.

steps.prompt: Moment 4: your own phone, which holds the platform’s device-bound passkey, is lost. The service still offers a backup sign-in method it supports. What now?

choices.text: Wait it out: biometrics make a lost phone useless to anyone else.
choices.consequence: Both the risk of misuse and the risk of lockout remain.
choices.explanation: A phone may also open with its PIN, and losing it can leave you locked out.

choices.text: Use the supported backup to sign in to the real service, revoke the lost phone’s passkey and review your sessions.
choices.consequence: You deal with the lost credential without trusting anyone’s link.
choices.explanation: Revoking and device controls differ between services, and a backup method is what lets you reach them.

blocks.debrief: Four separate situations, one routine: check the service before you register, keep the passkey on a device you control, count the older ways in, and decide beforehand what happens if the device is lost. Retry any choice you were unsure about.

questions.prompt: Which attack does a properly implemented passkey stop?

choices.text: Every scam once the account is open.
choices.explanation: A passkey has no opinion about payments, messages or anything else you do after logging in.

choices.text: A lookalike site collecting a valid sign-in response for the real service.
choices.explanation: WebAuthn ties the credential to the service’s identifier.

questions.prompt: Does “passkey” always mean a credential synced to the cloud?

choices.text: Yes; every passkey lives in one platform’s cloud.
choices.explanation: Physical keys and device-bound credentials exist too.

choices.text: No. Depending on the authenticator, it may sync or stay on one device.
choices.explanation: Where a passkey lives, and how it is backed up, depends on the authenticator.

questions.prompt: After adding a passkey, what should you check?

choices.text: Which old password and recovery routes the service still accepts.
choices.explanation: A weaker fallback can stay in place.
A face scan that opens the phone is only one part of how the account can be reached.
